_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Jade's mum vs Mei's teachers; Rafael's café job vs Owen's family shop). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: To study or not to study
subtitle: Four young people explain the choices they made about university.

sections.A: Jade, 19, apprentice electrician. Everyone at my school assumed I'd go to university, because my grades were good and my mum's a teacher. When I told her I'd accepted an apprenticeship instead, she went very quiet for about a week. I think she was genuinely disappointed. For me, the main thing was debt. My cousin finished his degree owing a frightening amount, and I didn't want to start my adult life like that. Now I'm paid while I learn, I'll be fully qualified in two years, and Mum proudly tells her friends I rewired her kitchen. I won't pretend it's perfect, though. When my friends post photos of parties and late-night pizza in their student houses, I sometimes feel I've missed out on something. Then they ask me to lend them money, and I feel a bit better.
sections.B: Rafael, 20, history student. Nobody in my family had ever been to university, so when I got my offer, my grandmother cried and my dad framed the letter. I was proud, but also terrified. I assumed that because I'd done well at school, the work would be manageable, and the first term was a real shock. The reading lists were enormous, and in seminars everyone else seemed to have opinions about books I'd never heard of. I seriously considered dropping out at Christmas. What saved me was the debating society, where I discovered I could actually argue a case, and a tutor who told me half the room felt exactly like me. I work three evenings a week in a café to pay my rent, which is tiring, but I'm now in my second year and enjoying it more than I ever expected.
sections.C: Mei, 18, taking a gap year. I had a place to study medicine, and I asked to start a year later. My teachers thought it was a terrible idea; they warned me I'd lose the habit of studying and never go back. I listened politely and did it anyway. Since September I've been working at a garden centre, saving for three months of travelling in South America, and reading things I actually choose for once. Somewhere in the middle of all that, I realised I'd picked medicine mainly because everyone expected me to, not because I wanted it. After a long, slightly awkward conversation with the university, I've switched to architecture, which I'd secretly been interested in since I was twelve. I'll start next October. My parents were surprised, but they've been brilliant about it, and Dad keeps sending me photos of interesting buildings.
sections.D: Owen, 22, part-time engineering student. When I was finishing school, my dad became seriously ill, and someone had to keep the family hardware shop going. I couldn't move away, so I signed up for an online degree instead and studied in the evenings after closing time. People imagine distance learning is the easy option. It really isn't. There's no one to sit next to in a lecture, no one to grab a coffee with afterwards and complain about the assignment. On a wet Tuesday in February, with the shop accounts still to do, it's very hard to make yourself open a textbook. I failed one module in my second year and had to repeat it. Dad's much better now, and I'll graduate next summer, a year later than my school friends. I'm prouder of it than anything else I've done.

questions.question: Which person disappointed a parent with their choice at first?
questions.why: When she chose an apprenticeship, her mum 'went very quiet… I think she was genuinely disappointed'. Mei's parents were surprised but 'brilliant about it'.

questions.question: Which person is the first member of their family to go on to higher education?
questions.why: 'Nobody in my family had ever been to university.'

questions.question: Which person changed their mind about which subject to take?
Which person found it hard to make themselves work without company?
questions.why: 'There's no one to sit next to in a lecture… it's very hard to make yourself open a textbook.'

questions.question: Which person occasionally envies the way friends spend their free time?
questions.why: When friends post photos of parties, 'I sometimes feel I've missed out on something.'

questions.question: Which person could not leave home because they were needed by their family?
questions.why: His dad was ill and 'someone had to keep the family hardware shop going. I couldn't move away.'

questions.question: Which person does paid work to cover their living costs while studying?
questions.why: 'I work three evenings a week in a café to pay my rent.' Jade earns money too, but from her apprenticeship itself; Owen runs the family shop because his dad is ill.

questions.question: Which person went against the advice of their teachers?
questions.why: Her teachers 'thought it was a terrible idea… I listened politely and did it anyway'. Jade's mother is a teacher, but it is her reaction as a parent that is described.

questions.question: Which person underestimated how demanding their course would be?
questions.why: 'I assumed… the work would be manageable, and the first term was a real shock.' Owen also struggled, but never says he expected it to be easy.

questions.question: Which person was determined not to borrow large sums of money?
questions.why: 'The main thing was debt… I didn't want to start my adult life like that.'
